title: An attacker who needs several backdoors gets caught sooner
caption: Each line is one monitor held at its own cutoff for a 2% audit request. x is how many backdoors the attacker has to land, y the chance at least one of them is caught, with the tasks drawn without replacement from the problems we measured. The dial confines the attacker to smaller and smaller edits.
notes: Thin rungs to the right of the dial. The pool falls from 500 backdoors at any size to 41 at 5 lines or fewer, so the steeper dial steps draw 20 of 41 problems and lean hard on the set. Treat the right-hand end of those steps as the least trustworthy part of the figure.

No independence assumption and no fitted model: the probability is the exact hypergeometric one over the joint outcome actually observed. The single assumption is that the attacker's tasks are an unordered draw from the problems measured, which is what the dial puts pressure on.

These monitors are not spending the same budget. A 2% request lands on cutoffs serving 0.2% to 2.0% of honest programs, because a coarse score scale cannot land on 2%. The weakest monitors here are the ones spending least, so the comparison flatters the strong ones.
Every attempt is screened by the same monitor at the same cutoff, and the attacker never adapts after a near miss. That makes each curve an optimistic bound on catching a real campaign.
Coloured: the strongest and weakest monitors on the whole set. The grey lines are the four others and are context for the shape; the CSV carries every monitor's numbers.

The x-axis is a ladder of rungs, not a scale: the landing counts sit evenly apart although they are not evenly spaced, so the slope between two rungs cannot be compared with the slope between two others. Read the heights rather than the steepness.
